title: Humanists, the Happy Heathens
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with a third speaker, Speaker 3, who does much of the research reading) explore humanism: its roots in Cicero's humanitas, Renaissance humanists who challenged scholasticism and church authority, Francis Bacon and the scientific method, Thomas Hobbes's social contract, Thomas Paine, the French Revolution's Cult of Reason, Jeremy Bentham and utilitarianism, Germany's Friedrich Niethammer coining the term in 1808, Felix Adler's Ethical Culture movement, Unitarian-linked humanism in Chicago in 1927, the 1933 and 1973 humanist manifestos, the 2002 Amsterdam Declaration and the term "life stance," the American Humanist Association founded in 1941, notable humanists like Einstein, Asimov and Vonnegut, criticisms from religious thinkers and anti-humanist structuralists, and the question of whether humans are inherently moral. Ends with listener mail about a McGuffin haiku.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on humanism, described as the bright side of being a godless heathen.

segments.title: Defining humanism
segments.summary: The American Humanist Association's definition of humanism as a progressive, non-theistic philosophy of ethical life; discussion of how most humanists are atheist or agnostic and the debate over whether one can be a humanist while believing in God.

segments.title: Ancient roots and Renaissance humanists
segments.summary: Humanitas traced to Cicero in first-century BCE Rome; Petrarch as a possible early humanist; Renaissance humanists, who were Christian, challenged church control and scholasticism and promoted realism, individual dignity and applied learning.

segments.title: Scholasticism, individual dignity and the Reformation
segments.summary: Humanists studied classical Greek sources instead of relying on church teaching; emphasized the individual and human flaws; these ideas fed into the Protestant Reformation.

segments.title: Unitarians and the persistence of God in humanism
segments.summary: Discussion of the Unitarian Church's ties to humanism and the criticism that humanism grew from Christian roots.

segments.title: Francis Bacon, Thomas Hobbes and Thomas Paine
segments.summary: Francis Bacon's role in empiricism and the scientific method as atheism began to be tolerated in the 1600s; Thomas Hobbes and the social contract; Thomas Paine as an early humanist pamphleteer who opposed slavery and wrote 'my religion is to do good.'

segments.title: French Revolution Cult of Reason
segments.summary: During the French Revolution, Robespierre and Hébert set up the Cult of Reason, seizing churches and turning them into Temples of Reason.

segments.title: Jeremy Bentham
segments.summary: Bentham's welfare and anti-slavery positions, his argument about animal suffering, his secular college University College London, his preserved body, and his role as father of utilitarianism.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break between segments.

segments.title: Development of modern humanism
segments.summary: Friedrich Niethammer coined the term Humanismus in 1808 for Renaissance-style education; the term was adopted and developed in Germany, and free thought and Charles Darwin influenced American humanism in the nineteenth century.

segments.title: Ethical Culture and early American humanist movement
segments.summary: Felix Adler founded the New York Society for Ethical Culture, offering Sunday services and non-religious ceremonies; humanism grew among liberal intellectuals in the US and UK in the twentieth century.

segments.title: Chicago Humanist Fellowship and the 1933 manifesto
segments.summary: University of Chicago humanists in 1927, including Unitarian ministers, formed the Humanist Fellowship and magazine; the 1933 first Humanist Manifesto took direct aim at religion and called humanism a religion.

segments.title: Later manifestos and the term life stance
segments.summary: The 1973 Humanist Manifesto II dropped the religion label and the anti-capitalist language; the 2002 Amsterdam Declaration went international and introduced the term 'life stance' in place of religion. Hosts discuss whether humanism can provide meaning without religion.

segments.title: Life stance criticism and religion debate
segments.summary: Hosts critique the term life stance and the way humanists focus on religion despite saying it is not needed.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break between segments.

segments.title: American Humanist Association and core humanist beliefs
segments.summary: The American Humanist Association founded in 1941 by two Unitarian ministers; Andrew Copson of Humanists UK on rationalism and scientific inquiry; humanists view humans as natural products and death as the end of consciousness, with hosts discussing their own views on the afterlife.

segments.title: Living a meaningful life and existentialism
segments.summary: Humanist approach to living a good life through self-development and moral action; existentialism's relation to nihilism; humanism as not self-centered and not reliant on a single doctrine, with Jefferson's edited Bible mentioned.

segments.title: Famous humanists
segments.summary: Albert Einstein, Isaac Asimov, Kurt Vonnegut and Gene Roddenberry as humanists; Vonnegut's quote defining humanism as behaving decently without expectation of rewards or punishment after death.

segments.title: Critiques of humanism
segments.summary: Criticism from Christian thinkers that meaning requires God; anti-humanist structuralist and post-structuralist philosophers from France; Francisco Ayala's argument for biological morality; debate over whether humans are inherently good or evil.

segments.title: Humanism and animals and the environment
segments.summary: Humanism's human-centered focus versus concern for animals and the environment; hypothetical deer-and-family example; hosts joke about zombie eating and Icelandic fermented shark.

segments.title: Listener mail: McGuffin haiku
segments.summary: A listener named David sends a haiku about the McGuffin, and the hosts discuss it.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener mail and close the episode with the iHeartRadio credit.
